action_criteria.expected_evidence: Active denervation with chronic neurogenic change in the tongue and cervical muscles, fibrillation potentials in mentalis and thoracic paraspinals, and early lumbosacral involvement; reduced CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute or chronic infarct, hemorrhage, mass or demyelinating plaque; symmetric corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity extending to the basis pontis is nonspecific and supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; including infarcts, which atrial fibrillation makes a relevant question, and brainstem lesions in this bulbar presentation; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cervical and thoracic spine and cord: no compressive lesion and no cord signal change.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 612 U/L (3.5x ULN); blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12, folate, ESR and CRP normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: FVC 68% predicted, SNIP 41 cmH2O and NIF -55 cmH2O are reduced; the NIF meets an AAN 2009 marker for NIV discussion.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic variant on the ALS gene panel; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Apixaban, metoprolol and lisinopril cleared against riluzole; the 1-2 nightly drinks flagged as an added hepatotoxicity risk to cut down; baseline and serial ALT/AST with riluzole stopped at ALT >5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established

He drinks 1-2 drinks nightly, which adds to the liver risk; apixaban, metoprolol and lisinopril do not interact with it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not delay the swallowing assessment in a patient who is already choking or coughing on food or fluids.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bulbar weakness spreading to both arms with upper motor neuron signs (brisk jaw jerk, pseudobulbar affect, limb hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs and a left Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Arrange a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment now (aspiration risk, safe food and fluid consistencies) and a dietetic review with baseline weight, and discuss gastrostomy early, while FVC is above 50% predicted. He lives alone: involve his son, who already helps with meals, and arrange occupational therapy and support at home.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now and discuss NIV: NIF -55 cmH2O meets an AAN 2009 marker of respiratory insufficiency; assess orthopnoea and overnight oximetry or capnography to time NIV, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Advise reducing alcohol (currently 1-2 drinks nightly) while taking riluzole; apixaban needs no change.

Screen cognition and behaviour with a validated ALS tool (such as the ECAS), and explain the pseudobulbar affect (involuntary laughing or crying) to the patient and family, offering symptomatic treatment if it is distressing.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk jaw jerk, pseudobulbar affect, limb hyperreflexia, bilateral Hoffman signs and a left Babinski sign with lower motor neuron involvement in the bulbar, cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in thoracic paraspinal muscles (bulbar-onset ALS phenotype).
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.
Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy or SBMA.
CK 612 U/L (3.5x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

Respiratory function is already reduced (FVC 68% predicted, SNIP 41 cmH2O, NIF -55 cmH2O), and the NIF is weaker than -60 cmH2O. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).
Bulbar involvement carries a worse prognosis and an aspiration risk; swallowing assessment and early gastrostomy discussion, while FVC is above 50% predicted, are priorities.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. P is a 65-year-old right-handed retired accountant who presents with a 7-month history of progressive dysarthria and dysphagia. He initially noticed his speech becoming slurred and soft approximately 7 months ago, which he attributed to dry mouth from his medications. He himself noted that his voice had changed quality, becoming nasal and strained, and this was also remarked upon by his adult children during visits. Over the past 4-5 months, he has had increasing difficulty swallowing solid foods and has had multiple episodes of coughing after drinking thin liquids.

Concurrently, he has noticed progressive bilateral arm weakness over the past 5 months. He has difficulty opening jars, cutting food, and typing on his computer. He has noticed visible twitching in his arms and has developed painful cramps in his hands and forearms at night. His son has also noted twitching in his tongue.

He has a background of atrial fibrillation, and his cardiologist initially considered whether an embolic event could explain the symptoms before referring him to neurology. He has mild lower extremity weakness noted on examination by his internist 3 months ago, which has not clearly progressed. He has no sensory symptoms, no diplopia, and no bladder or bowel changes.

He lives alone since his wife's passing 2 years ago and is concerned about his ability to manage independently. His son has been helping with meal preparation.
